notes: Rent-control succession/family-member dispute (daughter passing on apartment); no compensated lodging or boarding-house issue.
Tenant-in-common vs. cotenant's commercial lessee dispute over business premises; no lodging/boarding issue.

court: Civil Court of the City of New York
notes: Loft Law 'residential occupant' priority dispute between prime tenant and one-year subtenant of loft space; not about lodging/boarding characterization.
Criminal larceny/extortion prosecution of landlords for forcibly evicting tenants; discusses license-vs-lease property theory only as analogy, not an actual lodging arrangement.
Overcrowding-statute/primary-residence dispute over tenant's daughter as additional occupant; not compensated lodging or boarding regulation.
Zoning challenge to floating-home (houseboat) district ordinance; concerns mobile-home/vessel zoning, not lodging or boarding.
Commercial holdover; dispute over use-and-occupancy liability after lease expiration and tender of keys. No lodging issue.

court: Supreme Court, Appellate Term, First Department
notes: Roommate-law (RPL 235-f) applicability to an incarcerated tenant's absent-roommate arrangement; no compensated short-term lodging at issue.

court: Justice Court of the Village of Port Chester
notes: Criminal trespass prosecution over nursing-home visitation restriction; unrelated to lodging or boarding.

holding_summary: The court held that the YMCA's residence, which provides rooms to transient guests at a daily rate (with some weekly long-term residents), is a 'hotel' within the meaning of General Business Law § 206, but the tenant's overcharge counterclaim failed because the statute only requires rates to be posted in public areas, not in each bedroom, and respondent failed to prove the posted public-area rates were exceeded.

quotes.text: Petitioner operates a “residence” that provides rooms for transient guests. The basic rental is a daily rate although there are 130 long-term residents who rent by the week, either as “students” or as “permanent” residents.
Without doubt, petitioner’s establishment is a “hotel” within the meaning of General Business Law § 206.
A more modern interpretation of the term “hotel” includes any place where “transient guests are received and lodged.”

court: Civil Court of the City of New York
holding_summary: The occupant originally paid the rent-controlled tenant $60/month for a room and handled his own cooking and cleaning, but the court held that decades of shared family life transformed the relationship into a true family unit, rejecting the landlord's argument that he remained a mere 'boarder' and awarding him succession rights under the rent-control regulations.

quotes.text: Originally the arrangement was that Jimmie would pay $60 per month for a room in the apartment. He would buy his own food and supplies, and do his own cooking and cleaning.
However, I do not accept this designation. It is obvious to me that Mr. Hendrix’s relationship changed radically in the 25 years he lived in apartment 25.

notes: Initial paying-lodger period spanned roughly a decade before evolving into a family relationship; no clean nights/weeks/months bucket fits, hence 'unclear'. Core holding is about family succession, not about the legality of the original room-letting arrangement.
Zoning variance dispute over a group home's second kitchenette ('housekeeping unit' definition); no compensated lodging or letting issue.

holding_summary: The tenant, unemployed and needing help paying rent, advertised for and took in a paying roommate for close to a year; the court held this did not constitute an illegal sublet requiring landlord consent because Real Property Law § 235-f protects an occupant and dependent children in the apartment regardless of any financial arrangement between tenant and roommate.

quotes.text: The respondent advertised for and secured a roommate to share his apartment and pay him money for the use of the apartment. This kind of arrangement existed for close to a year.

This provision does not prohibit the making of financial arrangements between the roommate and the tenant. It does however permit one occupant and that occupant’s dependent children to reside in the apartment without the landlord’s consent.
the occupants complained of are occupants fully protected by section 235-f of the Real Property Law.

notes: Court declines to characterize the paid-occupancy arrangement as lease or license, treating it as a statutorily-protected 'roommate' category.

holding_summary: The court held that because the Rules of the City of New York define 'transient occupancy' more narrowly (occupancy by the same persons for 90 days or less) than the Administrative Code's J-1/class-B hotel definitions (day-to-day or week-to-week accommodation), the prosecution could not rely on the building's authorized certificate-of-occupancy classification alone to establish transient use, and had to plead facts of actual or arranged 90-day-or-less lodging; having failed to do so, the fire-safety-director information was dismissed.

quotes.text: Such buildings shall include but are not limited to buildings occupied as hotels, motels, lodging houses, dormitories and single room occupancies.

buildings or parts thereof which contain a total of more than 30 sleeping rooms or can accommodate a total of more than 30 lodgers, or contain more than 15 sleeping rooms or can accommodate more than 15 lodgers above the first or ground story, used for living or sleeping purposes by the same person or persons for a period of ninety days or less shall be considered as being occupied by a transient occupancy.
Having failed to allege that the building here was used or arranged to be used for lodging of the same persons for 90 days or less, the information is legally deficient and is, therefore, dismissed.

notes: Regulatory scheme for lodging/transient-occupancy buildings is discussed at length and sustained in principle, though this particular prosecution failed on pleading grounds.
Installment land-sale contract labeled 'landlord-tenant' by its terms; court holds it is a contract-vendee relationship, not a summary-proceeding-eligible tenancy. No lodging issue.

Case adjudicates whether a funeral home qualifies as a customary 'home occupation'; the ordinance's definitional list separately names 'Bed and Breakfast Home' as a permitted home occupation, but that category is not litigated or discussed by the court -- a passing background reference only.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: Former building owners who sold to plaintiff and stayed on rent-free as owner-occupants sought Loft Law 'residential occupant' protection; court finds they are not tenants/lodgers at all. No compensated letting.
